title: Seven Days with the Bhagavad Gita
shortDescription: One week inside Hinduism's most beloved conversation: Arjuna's crisis, Krishna's counsel, and what it means for your life.
longDescription: The Bhagavad Gita is a 700-verse conversation between the warrior Arjuna, frozen at the edge of an impossible choice, and Krishna, his charioteer and friend. In seven daily text messages, this program walks you through the Gita's setting, its core teachings on action, duty, the mind, equality, and devotion, and helps you build a small ongoing Gita practice — while honestly noting where the great commentators disagree.
sourcePolicy: Content summarizes mainstream scholarly and traditional understandings; verse citations are to widely available translations.

lessons.title: Arjuna's crisis
lessons.learningObjective: Understand the Gita's opening situation and why it begins with a good person's breakdown rather than a sermon.
lessons.standardMessage:
7 DAYS WITH THE GITA — DAY 1 OF 7
ARJUNA'S CRISIS

The Bhagavad Gita does not open with peace. It opens with a panic attack.

Arjuna, the greatest warrior of his age, rides out between two armies about to fight a civil war. On the other side he sees his cousins, his teachers, his grandfather. His bow slips from his hand. His mouth goes dry. He tells his charioteer, Krishna, that he cannot fight — every option looks like ruin (chapter 1).

Then comes the hinge of the whole text (2.7): overwhelmed and "confused about dharma", Arjuna stops arguing and asks for help: teach me.

The Gita's first lesson isn't a doctrine. It's that wisdom begins when a capable, decent person admits: I don't know what's right.

Reflection: Where in your life are you between two armies?
Want the deeper meaning, a version for your kids, or the sources? Just ask.
lessons.deeperMessage:
The setting matters. The Gita sits inside the Mahabharata, just before the war of Kurukshetra — the catastrophic climax of a family feud in which the virtuous side has exhausted every peaceful option. Arjuna's collapse (1.28–47) is described physically: trembling limbs, burning skin, a reeling mind. The text takes despair seriously; it does not mock it.

Notice what Arjuna's arguments are. He isn't lazy or cowardly — he makes moral arguments: killing kin will destroy the family, corrupt society, and can't be worth any kingdom. They're good arguments. Krishna's response, unfolding over 18 chapters, doesn't dismiss them; it reframes the whole question — from "what will I get or lose?" to "what is mine to do, and who is the I that acts?"

Interpreters differ on how literally to take the battlefield. Traditional commentators (Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva) treat the war as real and Arjuna's duty as a kshatriya (warrior) as the concrete occasion for universal teaching. Gandhi read the battlefield as an allegory of the struggle inside every heart — and drew nonviolence from it. Either way, the Gita's staging makes one claim clearly: the deepest spiritual questions don't arise on quiet mountaintops. They arise in the middle of life, when duty, love, and fear all pull at once.
lessons.childMessage:
The Gita begins with a surprise: a mighty hero gets scared! Arjuna is the best archer in the world, but before a big battle he looks across the field, sees people he loves on the other side, and freezes. He can't move. He can't decide. So he does the bravest thing of all — he turns to his friend Krishna and says, "I'm confused. Please help me." Asking for help when you're stuck isn't weak. It's how wisdom starts.

Ask your child: When you feel stuck or scared, who can you ask for help?
lessons.sourceNote: Arjuna's breakdown is Bhagavad Gita chapter 1 (especially 1.28–47); his physical symptoms at 1.29–30; his plea "I am confused about dharma... teach me" is 2.7. The allegorical reading is documented in Gandhi's writings on the Gita; the literal-occasion reading reflects the classical commentaries. All citations are to real, widely translated verses.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Where in your life are you between two armies?
lessons.practicalAction: Name one decision you've been avoiding, and say out loud — to yourself or someone you trust — "I don't know what's right here."

lessons.title: Action without attachment
lessons.learningObjective: Understand Gita 2.47 — acting fully while releasing claim on results — as the heart of karma yoga.
lessons.standardMessage:
7 DAYS WITH THE GITA — DAY 2 OF 7
ACTION WITHOUT ATTACHMENT

Today, the Gita's most famous verse (2.47): "You have a right to your actions, but never to the fruits of your actions. Do not make the results your motive — and do not cling to inaction either."

Notice what this does NOT say. It doesn't say results don't matter, or that you shouldn't plan. It says: your job is the action; the outcome is woven from a thousand threads you don't control. Work wholeheartedly, then release your grip.

Athletes know this: focus on the shot, not the scoreboard, and you play better. The Gita calls this karma yoga — and adds a promise (2.48): evenness of mind in success and failure is itself yoga.

Reflection: What would you do differently today if you truly owned the effort but not the outcome?
Want the deeper meaning, a version for your kids, or the sources? Just ask.
lessons.deeperMessage:
Why should letting go of fruits improve action rather than gut it? The Gita's psychology: craving for results splits your attention (half on the work, half on the reward), breeds anxiety before, distortion during, and either arrogance or despair after. Action offered without that fever is cleaner, steadier, and — crucially for the Gita — doesn't bind you. Chapter 3 adds that no one can actually renounce action (3.5: even staying alive is action), so the choice isn't between acting and not acting, but between acting anxiously and acting freely. Krishna also names a social dimension, lokasangraha (3.20): the wise keep acting for the world's well-being, as examples for others.

The commentators frame 2.47 differently. For Shankara (Advaita), karma yoga purifies the mind, preparing it for the liberating knowledge that the Self was never the doer — knowledge, not action, finally frees. For Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), desireless action performed as worship of God is itself a limb of devotion. Later teachers like Vivekananda and Gandhi made 2.47 an ethic of tireless, selfless public work. Same verse, different architectures — but all agree on the practical core: full effort, open hand.

Try it as an experiment, not a belief: pick one task today and do it completely, while consciously dropping the inner commentary about credit, praise, and payoff. Notice what changes.
lessons.childMessage:
Krishna teaches Arjuna a trick that great athletes and artists use: put your whole heart into DOING your best, and don't spend the whole time worrying about winning. When you shoot a basketball, if you're thinking "what if I miss? what will everyone say?" — your arms get wobbly! But if you just focus on the shot, you do better and it's more fun. Your effort belongs to you. The result has to share itself with luck, other people, and the whole world.

Ask your child: What's something you love doing even when you don't win?
lessons.sourceNote: Bhagavad Gita 2.47 ("karmany evadhikaras te ma phaleshu kadachana...") and 2.48 ("samatvam yoga uchyate") are real, famous verses; 3.5 and 3.20 (lokasangraha) are also authentic. The contrasting Advaita and Vishishtadvaita framings summarize Shankara's and Ramanuja's extant Gita commentaries. The sports analogy is this lesson's own illustration, not scripture.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What would you do differently today if you truly owned the effort but not the outcome?
lessons.practicalAction: Choose one task today and do it start to finish without checking for praise, likes, or credit afterward.

lessons.title: What is your duty?
lessons.learningObjective: Understand svadharma — the Gita's teaching that your own duty, however imperfect, beats a borrowed life.
lessons.standardMessage:
7 DAYS WITH THE GITA — DAY 3 OF 7
WHAT IS YOUR DUTY?

The Gita's answer to "what should I do?" starts with a striking verse (3.35): "Better is one's own dharma, though imperfectly done, than the dharma of another done perfectly. Better to die in one's own dharma; the dharma of another invites danger."

This is svadharma — "own-duty": the responsibilities that arise from who you actually are — your abilities, your roles, your stage of life, your circumstances. Not your cousin's path, your parents' script, or the internet's highlight reel.

For Arjuna, a warrior at a battle for justice, svadharma meant standing his ground. Yours looks different. The question the Gita hands you is precise: given who I am and where I stand, what is mine to do?

Reflection: Where are you doing someone else's dharma well instead of your own imperfectly?
Want the deeper meaning, a version for your kids, or the sources? Just ask.
lessons.deeperMessage:
The Gita returns to this at the very end (18.47, nearly repeating 3.35) and adds a generous note at 18.48: every undertaking has defects, "as fire is covered by smoke" — so don't abandon the work that fits your nature just because it's flawed.

An honest complication: in its original setting, svadharma included Arjuna's duty as a member of the warrior class, and classical readers heard varna (social class) in it. Modern teachers tend to universalize the principle: your svadharma flows from your svabhava — your actual nature, aptitudes, and commitments (18.41–45 links duty to qualities, guna-karma, rather than simple birth in many modern readings; traditional readings differ, and it's fair to say interpreters genuinely disagree here).

What's not in dispute is the psychological insight. A life spent performing someone else's role — the career chosen to please, the personality worn to fit in — corrodes from inside, however polished it looks. The Gita's counsel pairs with day 2: discover what is yours to do (svadharma), then do it without clutching at results (karma yoga). Together they form a livable ethic: deeply engaged, weirdly free.

A practical test some teachers suggest: your svadharma is usually found where your abilities, your responsibilities, and the world's genuine need overlap — and it often feels less like glamour and more like quiet fit.
lessons.childMessage:
Krishna tells Arjuna: it's better to be YOU — even an imperfect, still-learning you — than a perfect copy of somebody else. A fish shouldn't feel bad that it can't climb trees, and a monkey shouldn't feel bad that it can't breathe underwater! Everyone has their own part to play, their own "dharma". Your part might be different from your friend's part, and that's exactly how it should be.

Ask your child: What is something YOU are good at that feels like your special part to play?
lessons.sourceNote: Bhagavad Gita 3.35, 18.47, and 18.48 (fire covered by smoke) are real verses; 18.41–45 connects duties to qualities and actions. The note that classical commentators read svadharma within the varna framework while many modern teachers universalize it by aptitude is an honest summary of a genuine interpretive disagreement, not a single-source claim. The fish/monkey image is a modern illustration, not scripture.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Where are you doing someone else's dharma well instead of your own imperfectly?
lessons.practicalAction: Write one sentence: "Given my abilities and responsibilities right now, the thing that is clearly mine to do is ___" — and do one step of it.

lessons.title: Training the mind
lessons.learningObjective: Learn the Gita's sixth-chapter teaching that the restless mind can be trained through practice and detachment.
lessons.standardMessage:
7 DAYS WITH THE GITA — DAY 4 OF 7
TRAINING THE MIND

In chapter 6, Arjuna makes a confession that sounds like it was texted from this century (6.34): "The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful, stubborn, Krishna — restraining it seems harder than controlling the wind."

Krishna's reply is kind and practical (6.35): yes, the mind is hard to restrain — but it can be done, through abhyasa (steady practice) and vairagya (letting go). Not through force. Through repetition and release, like training a puppy: it wanders, you gently bring it back, a thousand times.

The same chapter says the self can be its own best friend or worst enemy (6.5–6) — and prescribes moderation: yoga is not for those who eat, sleep, or work too much or too little (6.16–17).

Reflection: What does your mind do when you finally sit still?
Want the deeper meaning, a version for your kids, or the sources? Just ask.
lessons.deeperMessage:
Chapter 6 contains the Gita's most concrete meditation instructions: a steady seat in a clean place, body and head aligned, gaze settled, mind gathered on a single point, practicing steadily without wanting a prize from the sitting itself (6.10–14). The promised result isn't fireworks; it's a mind "like a lamp in a windless place" (6.19) — one of the most loved images in Hindu literature.

The two-tool prescription of 6.35 became foundational far beyond the Gita: Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (1.12) uses the identical pair — abhyasa and vairagya — as the method for stilling the mind's churn. Practice means showing up regularly, at whatever small scale you can sustain; detachment means dropping the tug-of-war with thoughts rather than winning it.

And the Gita is tender toward failure. When Arjuna asks what happens to someone who tries and doesn't get far (6.37–40), Krishna answers: no sincere effort is ever lost — "no one who does good, dear friend, ever comes to a bad end." Schools differ on meditation's place: Advaita treats it as preparing the mind for liberating knowledge; devotional schools fold it into remembrance of God (the chapter itself ends, 6.47, calling the one who worships with faith the most complete yogi). But every school keeps the core counsel: start small, be regular, be gentle, don't quit.
lessons.childMessage:
Even the hero Arjuna told Krishna: "My mind jumps around like crazy — controlling it is like catching the wind!" Krishna didn't laugh. He said: you're right, minds are jumpy — but they can learn to settle, with practice and patience. Training your mind is like training a puppy. The puppy runs off; you gently bring it back. Again and again. Slowly, the puppy learns to sit — and so does your mind. Even one quiet minute is real training.

Ask your child: Want to try sitting totally still and quiet with me for one whole minute?
lessons.sourceNote: Bhagavad Gita 6.34 (mind restless as wind), 6.35 (abhyasa and vairagya), 6.5–6 (self as friend/enemy), 6.16–17 (moderation), 6.10–14 (meditation posture), 6.19 (lamp in a windless place), 6.37–40 (the fate of the unsuccessful striver), and 6.47 are all real verses. Yoga Sutras 1.12 uses the same practice/detachment pair. The puppy-training analogy is a modern teaching illustration.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What does your mind do when you finally sit still?
lessons.practicalAction: Sit still for three minutes today; each time your mind wanders, gently return attention to your breath — no scolding.

lessons.title: Seeing the same Self in others
lessons.learningObjective: Understand the Gita's vision of equality — the same Self in all beings — and its ethical consequences.
lessons.standardMessage:
7 DAYS WITH THE GITA — DAY 5 OF 7
SEEING THE SAME SELF IN OTHERS

The Gita's ethics rest on a startling perception, not a rule. Verse 6.29: the person steadied by yoga "sees the Self in all beings, and all beings in the Self — seeing the same everywhere."

And 5.18 makes it concrete and social: the wise see "the same" in a learned scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste — the categories that ancient society ranked most sharply. The verse deliberately flattens the hierarchy.

This isn't a claim that everyone is identical in personality or talent. It's deeper: beneath every rank and role, the same conscious light looks out. Once you glimpse that, contempt becomes absurd — like your right hand sneering at your left.

Reflection: Who do you find hardest to see this way?
Want the deeper meaning, a version for your kids, or the sources? Just ask.
lessons.deeperMessage:
The Gita pushes the vision further: "the one who sees me everywhere, and sees everything in me — I am never lost to them, nor are they ever lost to me" (6.30). And it grounds compassion in it (6.32): the highest yogi measures others' joy and pain "by the same standard as their own" — the Gita's version of feeling-with.

The schools interpret the metaphysics differently, and it's worth knowing how. Advaita reads these verses literally: there is numerically one Self; separateness is misperception, so harming another is, in the deepest accounting, self-harm. Vishishtadvaita reads the sameness as all beings forming the body of one God — distinct souls, one divine indweller, equal dignity. Dvaita maintains eternally distinct souls who are equally dependent on and beloved of God. Notice: three metaphysics, one ethical output — no one is spiritually disposable.

Be honest about history: verses like 5.18 coexisted for centuries with steep social hierarchy, and reformers from bhakti saints to modern figures have wielded exactly these verses against caste contempt and exclusion. A text can be ahead of its society — and its society can take centuries to catch up. The practical discipline the Gita suggests is perceptual: practice looking at the annoying colleague, the stranger, the person you were taught to look down on, and silently noting — same light, different lampshade.
lessons.childMessage:
Krishna teaches Arjuna a special way of seeing. Imagine everyone in the world is wearing a costume — different faces, ages, languages, jobs. But inside every costume shines the very same kind of light. The wise person, Krishna says, sees that light in everyone: a teacher, an animal, a stranger, even someone others ignore. When you remember the light is in everyone, it gets very hard to be mean — and very easy to be kind.

Ask your child: Can you think of someone at school who might need you to see their light this week?
lessons.sourceNote: Bhagavad Gita 6.29, 6.30, 6.32, and 5.18 are real, widely translated verses; 5.18's list (scholar, cow, elephant, dog, outcaste) is in the text. The three schools' readings summarize the Vedanta commentarial traditions. The use of these verses by anti-caste reformers is documented history. "Same light, different lampshade" is a modern illustration, not scripture.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Who do you find hardest to see this way?
lessons.practicalAction: Pick one person you tend to dismiss and, next time you see them, silently note: "the same Self looks out of those eyes."

lessons.title: Devotion and surrender
lessons.learningObjective: Understand bhakti in the Gita — devotion as relationship and surrender as trust rather than defeat.
lessons.standardMessage:
7 DAYS WITH THE GITA — DAY 6 OF 7
DEVOTION AND SURRENDER

As the Gita deepens, its tone turns intimate. Krishna stops sounding like a philosopher and starts sounding like someone in love with the world. "Whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, fruit, or water with devotion — that offering of love I accept" (9.26). Not grandeur. Love.

Chapter 12 describes the devotee God holds dearest: friendly and compassionate to all, free of possessiveness, even-minded in pleasure and pain, forgiving (12.13–14).

And the Gita's final teaching (18.66): "Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone; I will free you from all faults — do not grieve." Surrender here isn't giving up. It's the trust of a child in a parent's arms: still climbing, but no longer climbing alone.

Reflection: What would you do differently if you truly believed you were not carrying life alone?
Want the deeper meaning, a version for your kids, or the sources? Just ask.
lessons.deeperMessage:
Bhakti — from a root meaning to share or participate — is devotion as relationship: God not as concept but as friend, parent, master, beloved. The Gita's bold move is Krishna's declaration that this path is open to absolutely everyone (9.32): women, vaishyas, shudras — everyone the old ritual system marginalized — "attain the supreme goal." Devotion needs no Sanskrit, no priest, no wealth: a leaf and love suffice.

How central is bhakti? Here the schools genuinely part ways. For Shankara (Advaita), devotion is a supreme purifier that ripens into knowledge — the final step is realizing non-difference from Brahman. For Ramanuja, 18.66 (the charama shloka, "final verse") is the summit of the entire Gita: surrender (sharanagati) to a personal God of infinite kindness is both the means and the joy of liberation; the Shri Vaishnava tradition built its theology on this verse. Madhva's Dvaita likewise crowns devotion, with souls eternally distinct from and delighting in God. Later bhakti movements — Chaitanya's Gaudiya tradition among them — made love of Krishna the whole of religion.

A modern note: surrender language can be misused, so hear the Gita's version precisely. Krishna asks Arjuna to release anxiety and self-importance, not responsibility — the very next verses send him back into action. Surrender, Gita-style, is doing your full duty with an unclenched heart, trusting that the universe's deepest current is benevolent.
lessons.childMessage:
Krishna tells Arjuna something wonderful: you don't need fancy gifts to be close to God. Even one leaf, one flower, or a little water — offered with love — makes God happy. It's like when you draw a picture for someone you love: the paper costs almost nothing, but the love makes it a treasure. And Krishna makes a promise: whoever trusts me doesn't have to carry their worries alone. Like a piggyback ride when your legs are tired — you're still on the journey, but someone strong is carrying you.

Ask your child: What tiny gift could you give someone today to show love?
lessons.sourceNote: Bhagavad Gita 9.26, 9.32, 12.13–14, and 18.66 are real, widely translated verses; 18.66 is revered in Shri Vaishnavism as the charama shloka. The differing weights given to bhakti by Shankara, Ramanuja, and Madhva summarize their commentaries; the etymology of bhakti (from bhaj, to share/participate) is standard. The reading of surrender as trust-plus-responsibility reflects mainstream traditional teaching.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What would you do differently if you truly believed you were not carrying life alone?
lessons.practicalAction: Make one small offering today with full love — a flower, a lit lamp, or a genuine thank-you to someone who carries you.

lessons.title: Building a Gita practice
lessons.learningObjective: Design a small, sustainable habit of reading and living the Gita beyond this week.
lessons.standardMessage:
7 DAYS WITH THE GITA — DAY 7 OF 7
BUILDING A GITA PRACTICE

In six days you've walked the Gita's arc: honest crisis (day 1), wholehearted action with an open hand (2), your own duty over a borrowed life (3), the trainable mind (4), the same Self in everyone (5), and love that carries you (6).

The Gita was never meant to be finished — it's meant to be revisited. A practice that works for many: one verse a day. Read it slowly, twice. Ask: what would today look like if this were true? Then live the day and check back at night.

Start with chapter 2 (the summary chapter) or chapter 12 (the shortest, on love). Keep a translation you enjoy within arm's reach. Small and daily beats heroic and abandoned.

Reflection: Which of this week's six teachings does your life most need right now?
Want the deeper meaning, a version for your kids, or the sources? Just ask.
lessons.deeperMessage:
Some guidance for the road. On translations: there are hundreds, and they differ because interpretation differs. Eknath Easwaran's is warm and readable; Winthrop Sargeant's gives word-by-word Sanskrit; Swami Gambhirananda translates with Shankara's Advaita commentary; translations from ISKCON (Prabhupada) read through Gaudiya Vaishnava devotion. Reading two side by side is itself an education in how the tradition thinks — you'll watch Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and bhakti lenses refract the same Sanskrit differently, and that's a feature, not a flaw.

On method: the traditional rhythm is shravana (hear/read), manana (reflect until it's yours), nididhyasana (let it soak into how you act). A modern version: verse in the morning, one honest attempt to apply it by evening. Journal one line. The Gita itself blesses tiny beginnings: "even a little of this practice protects from great fear" (2.40), and no sincere effort is ever lost (6.40).

On community: the Gita came alive for Arjuna in conversation, not solitude. A study group, an online satsang, or even one friend on the same schedule multiplies staying power. And keep the endpoint in view: the Gita measures progress not in chapters read but in evenness of mind, kindness, and courage under pressure. When Arjuna finally says "my confusion is destroyed... I will act" (18.73), he doesn't become a scholar. He stands up.
lessons.childMessage:
You've now heard the Gita's whole story: Arjuna was scared, Krishna helped him understand — do your best, be yourself, train your jumpy mind, see the light in everyone, and remember you're never alone. At the very end, Arjuna stands up, brave again! The Gita isn't a book you read once, like a bedtime story. It's more like a wise friend you visit again and again, your whole life, with new questions each time.

Ask your child: If you could ask Krishna one question, what would it be?
lessons.sourceNote: Bhagavad Gita 2.40 ("even a little of this dharma protects from great fear"), 6.40, and 18.73 (Arjuna's resolution) are real verses. The named translations (Easwaran, Sargeant, Gambhirananda/Shankara, Prabhupada) are widely available and genuinely reflect different interpretive traditions. Shravana-manana-nididhyasana is a classical Vedantic learning method (rooted in Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5). Practice suggestions are this course's own synthesis.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which of this week's six teachings does your life most need right now?
lessons.practicalAction: Get a Gita translation this week, put it where you'll see it daily, and read one verse tomorrow morning.
